title: Password Security Basics Every Small Business Owner Needs to Know
excerpt: Weak passwords remain the number one way criminals break into small business accounts and systems. Learn simple, practical steps to protect your company without expensive software or technical expertise.
content_html:
Every week, small businesses lose money, customer data, and their reputation because someone used a weak password. The good news? Fixing this problem is one of the easiest and cheapest security improvements you can make today.

Why Passwords Matter More Than You Think

Think of passwords as the keys to your business. You wouldn't leave your shop unlocked overnight, yet many businesses essentially do this digitally every day. Criminals use automated tools that can guess millions of common passwords in seconds. Once they're in, they can access your bank accounts, customer information, email, and everything else connected to that account.

Small businesses are actually targeted more often than large corporations because hackers know you're less likely to have dedicated security staff. A single compromised password can lead to fraudulent wire transfers, stolen customer data, and even ransomware that locks you out of your own systems.

What Makes a Password Strong

Forget everything you learned about replacing letters with numbers. P@ssw0rd123 is not secure. Modern strong passwords follow these principles:

  • Length beats complexity: A password like "correct-horse-battery-staple" is far stronger than "Tr0ub4dor&3" and easier to remember. Aim for at least 16 characters.
  • Unique for every account: Never reuse passwords. If one service gets hacked, criminals immediately try that password on banks, email, and other valuable targets.
  • Avoid personal information: Your dog's name, birthday, or street address are easy for criminals to find on social media.

Start Using a Password Manager Today

Nobody can remember dozens of unique 16-character passwords, and you shouldn't try. Password managers are simple apps that create, store, and fill in strong passwords automatically. You only need to remember one master password to unlock the vault.

Most password managers cost between five and ten pounds per person monthly for business plans. This small investment eliminates sticky notes on monitors, passwords in spreadsheets, and the constant "forgot password" cycle that wastes everyone's time.

Popular options include 1Password, Bitwarden, and Dashlane. Many offer free trials so you can test before committing. Set aside one afternoon to move your team's most important accounts into the manager, then gradually add others.

Add Two-Factor Authentication Everywhere Possible

Two-factor authentication, often called 2FA, adds a second check beyond your password. Usually this means entering a code from your phone or approving a notification. Even if a criminal steals your password, they can't get in without that second factor.

Enable 2FA immediately on these accounts:

  • Email (this is the master key to everything else)
  • Banking and financial services
  • Cloud storage like Google Drive or Dropbox
  • Social media accounts
  • Any system containing customer data

Most services offer 2FA in their security settings. Authenticator apps like Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator are more secure than text message codes, though text messages are still better than nothing.

Create a Simple Password Policy for Your Team

Write down basic rules everyone must follow and review them during onboarding. Keep it simple: use the password manager for everything, never share passwords via email or chat, and report any suspicious login attempts immediately. When someone leaves the company, change shared passwords that day.

Password security isn't glamorous, but it's the foundation everything else sits on. Spend a few hours this week setting up a password manager and enabling two-factor authentication on critical accounts. These simple steps will dramatically reduce your risk of becoming another small business cybercrime statistic.

title: Free Microsoft 365 & Google Security Checks You Can Run Today
excerpt: CISA's free SCuBA tools let small businesses secure Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace without hiring consultants. Learn how to run these automated checks and fix the settings that actually stop breaches.
content_html:
If you've ever looked at a cybersecurity framework and felt overwhelmed, you're not alone. Most security guidance was written for companies with dedicated IT departments and six-figure budgets. The good news? CISA (the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) built something specifically for the rest of us: SCuBA, which stands for Secure Cloud Business Applications. It's free, it works with Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace, and you can run it this afternoon.

Why Most Security Frameworks Miss the Mark for Small Teams

Enterprise frameworks like the full NIST Cybersecurity Framework or comprehensive CIS Controls contain hundreds of recommendations. They're thorough, but they assume you have a team to implement them. The result? Many small business owners either ignore security entirely or check random boxes without understanding what actually matters.

Here's what the data shows: According to the Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report, the vast majority of breaches affecting small businesses come from stolen credentials (login details), phishing emails, and misconfigured cloud settings. You don't need to implement 200 controls—you need to nail the 15 that cover 90% of real-world attacks.

What SCuBA Actually Does

SCuBA is a set of free tools that automatically check your Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace settings against security best practices. Think of it as a health check-up for your email and cloud apps. It looks at things like:

  • Whether multi-factor authentication (requiring a second verification step beyond your password) is enabled for all users
  • If email forwarding rules could be sending copies of your messages to attackers
  • Whether external file sharing is too permissive
  • If administrator accounts have proper protections

These checks align with what security experts call "Implementation Group 1" in the CIS Controls v8—the baseline protections every organisation should have regardless of size. They also map to Australia's ACSC Essential Eight framework, specifically the foundational Maturity Level 1 controls.

How to Run Your First SCuBA Assessment

You'll need someone comfortable with basic computer administration, but you don't need to be a programmer. Here's the process:

  • Step 1: Visit CISA's SCuBA GitHub page and download the ScubaGear tool (for Microsoft 365) or ScubaGoggles (for Google Workspace)
  • Step 2: Run the tool while logged in as an administrator of your cloud account
  • Step 3: Review the generated report, which shows you exactly which settings don't meet security baselines
  • Step 4: Work through the findings one at a time, starting with anything marked as high priority

The reports explain each issue in plain language and tell you exactly where to find the setting that needs changing. Most fixes take less than five minutes once you know where to look.

Focus on What the Frameworks Agree On

Whether you're following NIST CSF 2.0's guidance on building an Organizational Profile for small businesses, or working toward the Essential Eight's Maturity Level 1, the priorities are remarkably consistent. Protect login credentials. Control who can access what. Make sure your email isn't an open door for attackers.

SCuBA doesn't replace a comprehensive security strategy, but it gives you an immediate, concrete starting point. It turns vague advice like "harden your cloud environment" into a specific checklist you can act on today.

Your Next Steps

Security doesn't have to be paralysing. Run a SCuBA assessment this week. Fix the top three issues it identifies. You'll have accomplished more meaningful security work than many businesses that spend months studying frameworks without taking action. The tools are free, the guidance is clear, and the protections are real. That's exactly what small business security should look like.
